content:
Earlier this year, I replaced my battery-powered mower with an iPhone-controlled robotic mower. When using that machine, you need to manually drive it around the perimeter of the yard to build a virtual map. Once everything is set up, it will automatically carry out mowing work according to a schedule.

Recently, I have been testing another system called the TerraMow V1000. It uses a completely different navigation method. After several weeks of testing, I believe it may be a more user-friendly choice for many people.

Camera-driven automatic mapping

The biggest difference between the TerraMow V1000 and the Anthbot M9 I reviewed earlier this year lies in how each machine understands your yard.

The Anthbot M9 uses an RTK reference station for positioning. Its setup process required me to manually drive the mower along the boundary on my iPhone to build the initial map.

The TerraMow V1000, on the other hand, uses a system the company calls TerraVision 2.0. With three cameras, the mower can automatically map the lawn and navigate without the need to bury boundary wires or set up a separate RTK antenna.

The automatic method did take longer to build my initial map. However, I think for people who are less inclined to "tinker" with their tech, this approach may be simpler.

To test this idea, I had my mum, who lives in another state, set up and use the TerraMow V1000 on her own without my help. She reported that everything worked fine. Though I'm not entirely sure she'd have the patience to manually drive a robot all the way around the boundary and then manually mark out the areas to avoid.

Automatic mapping did cause one small quirk in my front yard. There's no fence or other physical barrier between my lawn and my neighbour's, so TerraMow initially included part of their yard in my map.

I fixed the issue by marking the area as a no-go zone in the app. However, for lawns that don't have a visually clear dividing line, you may need to pay closer attention during the initial mapping process.

Viewing through the mower's cameras

The cameras on the TerraMow also deliver one of my favourite features. The iPhone app can show a live view of what the mower sees while it is working.

During testing, I used iPhone Mirroring on my Mac to keep that feed open in a large window. That way I could work indoors while watching the mower move around the back yard from its own perspective.

This feature isn't strictly necessary for automated mowing, but it makes the robot more fun to watch, and every now and then it also explains why it slowed down or avoided certain things. The Anthbot M9 doesn't offer an equivalent camera view.

The two iPhone apps are actually quite similar in many design concepts. Both let you schedule work, adjust mowing behaviour, create zones, mark areas to avoid, and remote-control the mower.

TerraMow has one particularly nice twist on that last feature. In addition to the traditional left-and-right virtual joysticks, its app also offers a one-handed control mode. You can hold your iPhone normally and steer the mower with your thumb.

Manually driving the mower with an iPhone isn't the main purpose of either system. Ideally, the robot should run on a schedule without any intervention. That said, TerraMow's joysticks are truly impressive when cleaning up missed patches.

Sometimes it almost feels like I'm telekinetically controlling the robot (in a good way). I can let my iPhone hang at my side, barely moving my thumb as I walk beside the mower, and the machine follows my commands.

Every robotic mower app should copy this control method.

A more aggressive mower

Overall, the TerraMow V1000 also feels more aggressive than the Anthbot M9. During testing, it cut closer to the ground and produced noticeably more noise while working.

I wouldn't describe TerraMow as loud. However, the difference between the two is still noticeable. The Anthbot runs extremely quietly and is easy to forget is operating, even when it's mowing after dark with its headlight on.

Because TerraMow relies on cameras for navigation, it needs daylight to work reliably. This makes daytime scheduling more important.

The V1000 itself feels solid and sturdy. It's also larger than the Anthbot M9. TerraMow includes a protective garage in the box that covers the charging base, while Anthbot's garage has to be purchased separately.

Most importantly, the TerraMow has performed consistently and reliably. I relied on it for several straight weeks without having to take over the routine mowing myself.

When adaptive mapping becomes a little too clever

The same visual intelligence that makes TerraMow easy to set up can occasionally backfire.

The mower continually adjusts its map based on what it sees. After each work session, saving those changes takes a while, during which you can't perform other operations in the app.

I also ran into an interesting edge case after several days of continuous rain. Puddles formed in parts of the yard, and TerraMow rightly avoided those areas during its next run.

Inside the skipped circular patch, the grass subsequently grew taller. After a while, the mower seemed to treat those taller blades as something to keep avoiding, so even after the ground dried, that area still wasn't cut.

I fixed the issue by using the remote-control feature in the app to manually drive the mower through the taller grass. Once it returned to normal lawn condition, automatic mowing resumed in that area as usual.

Regular trimming along the edges also helps TerraMow reach boundaries more reliably. Tall grass growing along indistinct edges might otherwise be treated as obstacles rather than as part of the mowing area.

Anthbot's approach feels less adaptive. It relies more heavily on the boundaries and obstacles I define myself. This takes more effort up front, but it also prevents the map from changing its mind and avoiding a patch of grass.

The 9to5Mac take

After using both systems, for most people I lean toward TerraMow's camera-based approach.

For me, burying boundary wires wasn't practical, and installing an RTK reference station would mean yet another piece of hardware to position, power, and maintain. TerraMow does away with both.

Its visual navigation isn't flawless. The initial mapping takes longer, an invisible property line needed manual correction, and its adaptive behaviour once mistook overgrown grass for a permanent obstacle.

These issues are all manageable. In return, the TerraMow V1000 delivers easier setup, reliable automatic mowing, a fun live camera view, and the best manual-control experience I've used in any robotic mower app.

I do enjoy gardening, but mowing is the repetitive part. Handing that chore off to a robot frees up more time for landscaping, edging, and detail work, while keeping the lawn tidy.

The TerraMow V1000 performs well enough at the job that I'd recommend it, especially for users who want robotic mowing without burying wires, installing an RTK antenna, or manually tracing out their entire yard with an iPhone.

The TerraMow V1000 currently sells for US$999 on Amazon, available after applying a US$200 coupon on the site. You can also find the product on TerraMow's official website.
